strengths: I like the motivation of this paper. It is convincing that 1) understanding _what_ differs between different neural representations is important, and 2) prior work has mostly overlooked this question (although a few papers that were not cited do address this question; see weaknesses).
The methods appear to be reasonable and I don't see obvious errors.
The paper delivers a tool that could increase interpretability of representational differences, because the differences can be visualized.

Several of the findings are interesting; I was especially intrigued by 1) the method can identify low similarity, high importance concepts, 2) middle layers show the greatest differences between different networks.

In general, I find this paper to be sufficiently well written and structured; with the presentation and detailed image visualization and captions to be commendable: Figures and their captions can be read standalone and still convey key contributions; which significantly enhances readability.
Moreover, the proposed method is described and visualized in a way that makes it much easier to grasp all relevant key aspects.

At the same time, the extension of works by Fel et al. seems sensible, and to the best of my knowledge, the use of a dictionary-based concept attribution method for __model similarity__ studies is novel.
Moreover, I very much appreciate the experimental breadth the authors followed to test the different potential usecases of RSVC.
The paper is well-written, easy to follow, and defines well the different stages of the method and the evaluation.

The idea of the paper is novel - instead of comparing functional similarity or direct similarity in representations, it uses a decomposition into "concepts" and compares the similarity between concepts. Instead of providing one similarity measure, this paper also demonstrates visually what are the concepts that make two models similar or dissimilar.

The paper provides a comprehensive study of the relations between concept similarity and concept importance to address the main possible limitation of using concepts - their non-straight-forward connection to the computation in the model.
The topic is of great interest. Providing interpretable model comparisons that go beyond model performance will be useful to practitioners.
The method goes beyond just measuring similarity, but provides interpretation for both similar and dissimilar concepts, something that is often overlooked in model comparison.
The example in Figure 2 is very convincing.
The proposed method for measuring similarity and dissimilarity is very intuitive.

The paper explores a new area which is representational similarity using visual concepts. Finding interpretable ways on how different networks are similar may offer valuable insights to the community.
weaknesses: The paper falls short of fully delivering on the central question of showing what visual concepts make two models similar or dissimilar.

There is only one figure (Fig 2) in the main paper that directly addresses this central question, and the visual concepts themselves are not clearly defined or easily interpretable, making it difficult to understand the nature of the differences.
The contribution is more of a tool rather than showing what is different between different nets; the paper would be stronger if the tool were used to provide new insights into the model differences.
Other results (Figs 3, 4, 5) are interesting but fall back into summary statistics and do not provide a detailed understanding of the specific visual concepts that differ between the models.
The paper does not demonstrate how the tool can be used to gain actionable insights into model behavior or performance.

It is unclear how valuable the tool is to the community; more validation of its usefulness and a demonstration of advantages over other ways of identifying representational differences would strengthen the paper.

Several relevant prior works are overlooked and should be discussed or compared to (e.g., Rosetta Neurons…, Understanding the Role of Individual Units…, Exploring Neural Networks with Activation Atlases…, and recent work on interpretability via sparse autoencoders).
Lack of sanity checks and proof of concepts: the authors directly apply their proposed methods on arbitrary model pairings without first firmly establishing the validity of the proposed approach.

Establishing a baseline is needed (e.g., using two models with highly likely or guaranteed concept similarity) to understand how visualizations change; currently it is much more difficult to relate computed values and their significance.
Studying variations away from the baseline by structurally varying it (different augmentations, data subsets, etc.) is required to understand how the proposed metric changes.
More clearly establish what extracted concepts actually look like; examples in Fig 1 are convincing but those in Fig 2 are less convincing, making it difficult to see any consistency.

Conceptual / Architectural Inconsistencies: resizing each concept proposal to the model’s input resolution and passing through the network may make the extracted concepts hold much less meaning with respect to the actual network.
It is not clear how RSVC avoids confounders unlike MCS; confounding elements could still produce similar concept coefficients.
Unclear guarantees that U_2-1 operates in the same basis as U_1 for direct replacement; learned maps in Eq. 4 are trained without guarantees that the bases between both models overlap.
Question whether RSVC uses surrogate models because the projection matrix is another learned linear model.
Need to discuss related work on linear predictors and disentangled representation learning, which should be cited to augment the short reference in related works.
Section 3.3 is fairly redundant and should either be excluded entirely or described in much more detail.

The approach might be sensitive to the concept extraction method; the choice of dictionary size k and L1 sparsity regularization affect granularity and interpretability, and a more thorough investigation of these parameters is needed.

Computational cost is not discussed; the trade‑offs between number of images needed for extracting concepts and training the linear mapping, as well as scaling with model size and dataset size, should be investigated.
Usability requires a human in the loop to manually inspect concepts, which is time‑consuming and subjective; methods to automate or semi‑automate the interpretation should be explored.

Missing related work: Dravid et al., Rosetta neurons (ICCV 2023) and Rombach et al., Network-to-network translation with conditional invertible neural networks (NeurIPS 2020); also note a typo in line 250 ('to' instead of 'too').
Some implementation details are missing.
Brainscore is described as comparing representations between two neural networks, but actually it compares activations in a network to macaque brain activations; the description is inaccurate.
Colour bars in Figure 3 and 4 would make the figures slightly clearer.
In Eq. 5, mentioning why L1 regularisation is used would make it clear to the reader.

The introduction is quite brief and fails to motivate the problem addressed; it could benefit from a discussion on why interpretability is important and why concepts are more useful than saliency maps or superpixels (LIME).

The paper does not provide the expected insights about what visual concepts are learned by a model and what differs as scale, data, and architecture are varied; it is unclear why the three experiments are interesting.
Figure 5 layer‑wise metrics across various models offer little additional insight over Raghu et al. 2021.
Figure 4 shows high importance features with high correlation between L2 and Pearson coefficients, which is somewhat obvious.
The abstract claims a practical tool to discover the cause of model failures, but this discussion is missing in the main text.
More detail is required on how patches are extracted (random sampling, number of patches, whether each patch is resized independently) as mentioned in lines L167‑L169.
It is unclear why there is a trade‑off between computational cost and error between the two techniques (lines L202‑L203).
Ambiguity about which metric $R^{\rho}$ or $R^{S}$ is employed (lines L201‑L211).
Eq. 2 matches columns due to lack of direct correspondence; a discussion of this matching would be helpful.
The tuning of $\lambda$ in Eq 1 (line L297) is not explained.
The rationale for fine‑tuning DINO and MAE models on NABirds (lines L348‑L349) is unclear.
Clarify how the correlation plots in Fig 2 are generated (are matrices flattened to 1D? what are the values of n and k?).
The descriptions and explanations of the grid‑like textures and hand/arms in Fig 2 are unconvincing.
Fig 3 introduces low, medium CI and concept similarities without precise definitions; precise definitions (e.g., top 5 % percentile) are needed.
The number of points in each subplot of Fig 3 is not reported.
The claim that model differences are largely driven by medium similarity, medium importance concepts is hard to believe given the heatmap centers near 0.
Fig 4 presentation would be clearer if separate plots for high importance and low importance were presented.
The relationship between $\Delta$Pearson and L2‑distance/KL as implied by Fig 4 is not easily deducible; more clarification is needed.
